analysis.one_liner: Cuts capital gains and estate taxes and adds a $500-per-child tax credit.
analysis.headline: Introduced by the Senate Finance Committee chairman with 37 Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Finance Committee and never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or any further action before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut several federal taxes. It created a $500 credit for each child (phased out for higher incomes), allowed taxpayers to exclude half their capital gains from income and to adjust old purchase prices upward for inflation before calculating tax, raised the estate tax exemption from $600,000 to $1 million over eight years, and gave large breaks to family-owned businesses. It also expanded retirement accounts, letting spouses without workplace plans contribute and letting people withdraw savings without penalty to start a business, pay for college, or survive long-term unemployment. The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and nothing further ever happened to it.
analysis.who_benefits: Middle-income families with children would gain the $500-per-child credit, which phases out starting above $110,000 for joint filers and is nonrefundable, so families owing little or no income tax would get nothing. Households that own stocks, businesses, or other appreciated assets would gain the most in dollars: half of capital gains would become tax-free, assets held over three years would get inflation-adjusted purchase prices, corporations would pay only 28% on capital gains, and estates would benefit from an exclusion rising to $1 million plus a new exclusion of up to $1.5 million (and half the excess) for family-owned businesses, 20-year installment payment, and a no-interest portion. Savers would gain from broader IRA eligibility, tax-free 'IRA Plus' accounts, and penalty-free withdrawals for business startups, long-term unemployment, and college costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with children, asset owners, large estates

how_it_helps.text: Creates a $500 nonrefundable tax credit for each qualifying child under 18, phasing down by $25 for each $1,000 of income above $110,000 (joint), $75,000 (single), or $55,000 (married filing separately).

Lets taxpayers other than corporations deduct 50% of net capital gains from income and, for assets held more than three years, adjust the purchase price upward for inflation before calculating gain — sharply lowering the tax on investment profits.

Raises the unified estate and gift tax exemption from $600,000 to $1 million over eight years, lets estates that are mostly family-owned businesses exclude up to $1.5 million plus 50% of the excess, extends estate tax installment payments from 10 to 20 years, and removes interest on part of the deferred tax.

Expands retirement savings: raises and eventually repeals IRA income limits, allows a nonworking spouse a full $2,000 deductible IRA, creates tax-free 'IRA Plus' accounts, and permits penalty-free withdrawals for business start-up costs, long-term unemployment, and higher education expenses.
Allows a capital loss deduction when a taxpayer sells a principal residence at a loss.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. The bill text contains no revenue-raising offsets, so the cost of the cuts would have fallen on the government's books as higher deficits or been made up by other taxpayers or offsetting spending cuts. Within the bill, the largest dollar benefits flow to households with appreciated assets and large estates rather than to wage earners.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal Treasury and general taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The capital gains deduction, inflation indexing, and corporate capital gains rate cut concentrate their benefits on households that own appreciated stock, businesses, and real estate; the child credit, by contrast, is capped at $500 per child and provides nothing to families with incomes too low to owe income tax.

The estate provisions only matter to the wealthiest estates: the exemption rises from $600,000 to $1 million, and the family-business exclusion (up to $1.5 million plus half the excess) applies only when such interests exceed half the estate.
The bill text includes no revenue offsets, so enacting it would have widened the deficit or required cuts elsewhere to pay for the tax reductions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The child credit and the IRA expansions are genuinely useful to working and middle-income families, and penalty-free withdrawals for education, unemployment, and startups are real help in hard times. But the heaviest dollar benefits — the 50% capital gains exclusion, inflation indexing, and the estate tax package — flow to households with large assets, and the bill specifies no way to pay for any of it. A fair assessment is that this is a broad tax cut in which the family-friendly pieces are real but comparatively small against provisions that would primarily reduce taxes on accumulated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator William V. Roth Jr., chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, introduced the American Family Tax Relief Act on January 21, 1997, with Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and other Republicans joining as original cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was its last action of any kind.
The bill accumulated 37 cosponsors, all Republicans, but the Finance Committee never marked it up, reported it, or scheduled any vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, existing capital gains and estate tax rates stayed in place, so the largest prospective beneficiaries — owners of appreciated assets and large estates — gained nothing from it, and the Treasury kept the revenue. Working families likewise never received the $500-per-child credit through this vehicle. Nobody's taxes changed because of this bill; the main effect of its death was simply preserving the status quo, which favored the Treasury over wealthy asset owners relative to the bill's passage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; asset owners' tax cuts never happened

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Republican — 37 senators joined sponsor Roth — and the bill died in the Republican-run Finance Committee without any vote, so no roll calls exist to measure the split.

industries.industry: Mutual funds and real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The bill would let inflation indexing flow through regulated investment companies and REITs to their shareholders and extend the capital gains deduction to fund distributions, improving after-tax returns for investors. Fund shareholders include many middle-income retirement savers, but the dollar gains would concentrate in the largest holdings.

industries.industry: Closely held and family-owned businesses (including farms)
industries.note: The estate package would exempt up to $1.5 million (plus half the excess) of family business value from estate tax, allow heirs 20 years to pay, and charge no interest on part of the deferred tax — but heirs who sell the business or stop participating face recapture. This mainly benefits owners of substantial family enterprises rather than the general public.

Cutting the capital gains rate roughly in half and indexing purchase prices would raise after-tax investment returns and encourage trading and asset sales, benefiting the investment business. The revenue forgone would be borne by other taxpayers or the deficit.
